title: In an authoritarian economy, Jensen Huang may be too big to fail | Robert Reich
text:
Jensen Huang has said he would return to Nvidia as its CEO if its board requests it.
“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang, who admitted being unfaithful to his wife, resigned from Nvidia last week. US intelligence agencies have identified one of his alleged lovers as a spy for China. If true, Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips may have found their way there.
Beyond the tabloid headlines lies a much bigger story – a US economy that’s become dependent on the initiatives and decisions of a few powerful men who are too big to fail.
We tend to think of government as being authoritarian, democratic or somewhere in between. For the last 22 months, we’ve witnessed what happens when the US government turns authoritarian.
An economy can also be described along the same continuum.
Throughout most of the last century, the US economy was fairly democratic. Decisions about what was produced and at what price reflected the judgments of tens of thousands of corporate executives, managers and small-business owners – all of whom were trying to respond to consumers and investors. Through labor unions, workers also had some say.
But the US economy has become far more authoritarian.
In recent decades, it’s become concentrated in the hands of a few giant corporations. Economies of scale have enabled those corporations to spread their fixed costs over many goods and services, and the US government has nearly abandoned antitrust (anti-monopoly) enforcement.
Labor unions have shrunk from representing over a third of private-sector workers in the 1950s to just 6% today.
More recently – over the last five years – something else has occurred, especially in big tech, that’s pushed the economy much further toward authoritarianism.
A handful of men – among them, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, Larry Ellison, Tim Cook and Jensen Huang – have not only become the richest people in the world, with significant political clout. They also control the direction and pace of technologies on which the US and the world depend.
These men are, in fact, the authoritarians of the new economy. They have unparalleled power over every aspect of the lives of Americans and millions of others around the world. And they have leveraged themselves to be, or seem, too big to fail.
The leverage works like this.
Nvidia’s value depends on Jensen Huang.
Hours after Huang’s resignation last Thursday, Nvidia stock dropped 10.3% in pre-market trading, erasing approximately $490bn of Nvidia’s value by the time the market opened.
Since the start of the leadership controversy at Nvidia on 8 November, the company has lost about $800bn in market value.
The AI industry, in turn, depends on Nvidia. Nvidia controls about 90% of the global market share of advanced AI chips. It has also become the major financier for the entire AI industry. Some call Nvidia the “central bank of AI”.
Nvidia’s $5tn market value (before 8 November) equaled about 8% of the total value of the S&P 500.
The US economy, in turn, depends on the AI industry. In the first quarter of 2025, the buildouts of datacenters using Nvidia chips accounted for 92% of US economic growth. Over the past two years, AI has been responsible for roughly half of America’s overall growth.
This huge leverage also works in reverse. Analysts fear that Nvidia’s collapse could cause the AI bubble to burst, triggering a failure that could threaten the entire US, if not also the world, economy.
Most Americans’ 401(k)s are invested in giant index funds tied to the Nasdaq and S&P 500. The Nasdaq and S&P 500, in turn, are based largely on 10 huge corporations. These 10 corporations are all connected to Nvidia. Together, they comprise about 37% of the value of the entire US stock market.
What all this means is Jensen Huang may be too big to fail.
More than 177,000 people have so far signed a “Stand with Jensen” open letter demanding that Nvidia’s board of directors “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Signers include Elon Musk; the Y Combinator president, Garry Tan; the Epic Games CEO, Tim Sweeney; and thousands of self-reported Nvidia employees.
Huang is discussing a possible return to the company, though the chair of the company’s board has said it’s not considering the move. One Huang ally talks of a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia CEO’s return, and garner support from Trump. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person told the Financial Times, adding that the efforts have Huang’s support.
Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang were reinstated as Nvidia CEO, adding that he thought Huang had “learned a big lesson”.
Exactly what “big lesson” did Trump have in mind? That it’s not a good look for the CEO of the US’s most valuable corporation to have a romantic relationship out of wedlock?
Or that such a CEO shouldn’t break the law by supplying America’s most advanced AI chips to China through a Chinese spy?
On Tuesday, it was announced that Huang has agreed to appear on 1 December before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee in transcribed interviews.
Even in an authoritarian economy, no CEO is above the law. Or is he? We may soon find out.
- Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK
